newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Appeal against Arab East Jerusalem Jewish enclave.
newsitem.headline: Appeal against Arab East Jerusalem Jewish enclave.

text.p: An appeal was filed on Sunday against a plan to build a new Jewish enclave in Arab East Jerusalem, blocking building until a decision is handed down, a spokesman for Israel's Jerusalem municipality said on Sunday.

Israel's Channel One Television said the Jerusalem District Appeal Committee would hear the appeal by two left-wing Jerusalem city council members on Monday and had to deliver a decision within 30 days.
"There was an appeal," Jerusalem municipality spokesman Haggai Elias told Reuters. But he said he was not sure how long the committee could take to give its decision.
The councillors who filed the appeal were not immediately available for comment.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan told Reuters he had little faith the appeal would succeed and that it "only postpones the problem, it doesn't solve it".

Irving Moskowitz, a Miami-based businessman who bankrolls Jewish settlement in occupied areas, was granted on Thursday a Jerusalem municipality permit to build some 70 Jewish homes in the 11,000-strong Arab neighbourhood of Ras al-Amoud.
Netanyahu was apparently taken by surprise by the go-ahead for the project -- which Arab leaders said could wreck peacemaking -- and said he was working to block the plan "at this time".

Relations between Israel and the Palestinians were already in crisis over Israel's breaking ground in March on the Har Homa settlement on a hilltop known to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim on the edge of East Jerusalem.
Bar-Illan said Netanyahu might still have to act against the project, perhaps by invoking public safety or national security.
A senior PLO official earlier on Sunday said Palestinians didn't believe Netanyahu truly opposed the Ras al-Amoud plan.
"He is trying to improve his image worldwide and give the Americans an excuse to continue pressing the Palestinians to accept Jabal Abu Ghneim," the official told Reuters.

In a bid to ward off right-wing criticism he had gone soft on Jerusalem, Netanyahu stressed Israel had the right to build anywhere it pleased in Jerusalem but said the timing of the Ras al-Amoud plan was problematic.
"No one should have the false impression that we have changed our policy," a cabinet statement quoted Netanyahu as telling his government after its weekly meeting on Sunday.
Israel occupied Arab East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and says it will never give up what it calls its "eternal, united capital".
Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state and say building for Jews there pre-empts final peace talks that have yet to begin in earnest.
